passage:
Alka, you know me. Bhupen doesn't do half-baked. So yes, it's week six and I haven't shot a single frame of the documentary, but look at this. Forty-two tabs of research on the Brahmaputra ferrymen. Three notebooks. Outline version eleven.
Version ten had the ghat interviews in the wrong order, and version nine didn't open strongly enough. I'm getting really close now. Maybe version thirteen.
Every evening I feel so productive, like I've worked hard all day. But... okay. When Professor Baruah asked for the first rough cut last Friday, I said I needed one more week of research. And when I imagine him watching my actual footage, with the whole class there, my stomach flips.
Research doesn't get marked. An outline can't look bad in front of people.
Huh. Listen to me. Is that why I'm on version eleven?

qa.q: Which outline version is Bhupen on?
qa.a: Outline version eleven.

qa.q: Why does research feel safer to Bhupen than shooting the documentary?
qa.a: Research can't be marked or look bad in front of the class, so preparing postpones the risk of being judged by Professor Baruah.

qa.q: What small step could Bhupen take this week?
qa.a: Bhupen could shoot one rough ghat interview and show it to Alka first, so the first reaction comes from a safe person.

qa.q: How might Alka see six weeks of tabs and notebooks?
qa.a: Alka may admire the effort but notice that nothing has been filmed, and gently wonder whether the research has become a place to hide.

grounding: Shows a young adult endlessly researching and refining an outline, with the preparation feeling productive while it postpones the risk of judgement.

passage:
I'm Neelam, Gargi's roommate, and for five weeks I've watched her "almost start" her internship application essay.
First she read every past winner's essay she could find. Then she made a colour-coded spreadsheet of their structures. Then she bought a book on persuasive writing and underlined half of it. Her outline is taped to our wall, and every night she moves the sticky notes around.
Yesterday I asked, "How much have you written?"
"Nothing yet, but the structure's nearly perfect." She sounded proud, even cheerful.
But when I offered to read a rough paragraph, she went very still. "Not until it's ready. I don't want anyone seeing a bad version."
I can't know what's going on in her head. From outside, it looks as if she's working all the time.
The deadline is Sunday.

qa.q: What did Gargi make after reading past winners' essays?
qa.a: A colour-coded spreadsheet of their structures.

qa.q: What does Gargi's 'I don't want anyone seeing a bad version' suggest about her preparation?
qa.a: It suggests Gargi is afraid of being judged; as long as she keeps outlining, no one can see a flawed draft.

qa.q: What could help Gargi move from outline to essay before Sunday?
qa.a: She could write one rough paragraph against a short timer and let Neelam read it, to see that a bad version isn't a disaster.

qa.q: What is it like for Neelam to watch the sticky notes move every night?
qa.a: Neelam sees constant effort but no writing, and seems quietly worried as Sunday nears, unsure how to help without pushing.

grounding: Illustrates, through a roommate's eyes, weeks of research and outline-polishing that feel like work but avoid writing a draft anyone could judge.

passage:
Hi Varun,
You asked how the research project is going. Honestly, I still haven't started writing. I've been "preparing" for five weeks.
I've read forty-two papers. I've rewritten the outline eleven times. Every time I finish it, I find something that could be better: a new source, a better structure. So I refine again. It feels productive. I tell myself I'm being thorough.
But last night I realised something. As long as I'm preparing, nobody can read my work and find it weak. The outline can't be judged if it never becomes a draft.
The deadline is in three weeks. Can you ask me on Friday if I've written the first page?
Mahima

qa.q: How many times has Mahima rewritten the outline?
qa.a: Eleven times.

qa.q: What did Mahima realise about the preparing?
qa.a: Mahima felt uneasy realising the endless preparing was a way to avoid the fear of being judged.

qa.q: What small step could help Mahima move from preparing to writing?
qa.a: Asking Varun to check in on Friday, and writing a rough first page before any more refining.

qa.q: How might Varun feel reading this email?
qa.a: Varun may feel sympathetic and glad to be trusted with the Friday check-in.

grounding: Shows a young adult refining an outline for weeks, feeling productive, while the preparation postpones the risk of being judged.

passage:
Ojas, you asked why I haven't sent you my short film script yet. Okay, confession time.
I started planning in January. I've watched maybe sixty films "for research". I've made mood boards. I've written character notes, twenty pages of them. I've changed the ending eight times in my head.
But the actual script? Zero pages.
Every time I sit down, I think, one more film, one more note, then it'll be ready. And it feels like work. It feels responsible.
But honestly? I think I'm scared. If I write it, someone might read it and think it's rubbish. As long as I'm still preparing, I'm still the guy with the brilliant idea. I'm Chinmay, and that's the truth.

qa.q: How many pages of character notes has Chinmay written?
qa.a: Twenty pages.

qa.q: What is Chinmay feeling underneath the preparation?
qa.a: Chinmay feels scared that someone will read the script and think it is rubbish.

qa.q: What could help Chinmay turn preparation into a script?
qa.a: Setting a short time limit to write a rough first scene, and sending it to Ojas even if it's messy.

qa.q: How might Ojas respond to this confession?
qa.a: Ojas might feel sympathetic and encourage Chinmay to share a rough page, promising to be kind.

grounding: Shows a young man endlessly preparing a script, which feels responsible, while avoiding the fear of being judged.

passage:
March: Francis started his final-year project on water purification. He made a research folder and read everything he could find.
April: The folder had grown to three hundred pages. His outline had five versions. His friend Pooja asked, "How's the draft?" "Almost ready to start," he said. He felt busy and important.
May: The deadline was three weeks away. Francis was still adjusting the outline, now version nine. Late one night, staring at the screen, he admitted to himself: if he never started the draft, his professor could never call it weak. He closed the outline, opened a blank page, and typed a clumsy first sentence.

qa.q: How many pages had Francis's research folder grown to by April?
qa.a: Three hundred pages.

qa.q: What was Francis feeling in April when he said "Almost ready to start"?
qa.a: He felt busy and important, as if preparing were real progress, which hid his fear of judgement.

qa.q: What turning point did Francis reach in May?
qa.a: He admitted the outline was protecting him from judgement, and typed a clumsy first sentence instead.

qa.q: How might Pooja feel when he keeps saying "almost ready"?
qa.a: Pooja might grow a bit worried or puzzled, noticing the draft never seems to begin.

grounding: Shows a student refining research and outlines for months, feeling productive, while postponing the risk of being judged.

passage: "Parul, you've been getting ready to start that blog for two months, so let your Dilnaz khala tell you something. When I was twenty, I wanted to enter a college essay competition on the history of our mohalla. I went to the library every day for six weeks. I filled three notebooks. I rewrote the outline eleven times; each version looked a little better and still not good enough to begin. I told everyone I was researching, and it felt so productive, like real work. The deadline came. I had a beautiful outline and not one paragraph. My friend Ruksana, who had started writing in week one with half my notes, won second prize. I cried, and then I understood: all that preparing was a way of never being judged. Start ugly, beta. Then fix."

qa.q: How many times did Dilnaz rewrite the outline?
qa.a: Eleven times.

qa.q: How did all the researching feel to young Dilnaz at the time?
qa.a: It felt productive and safe, like real work, while quietly hiding her fear of being judged.

qa.q: What choice inside the story could have changed the result?
qa.a: Starting to write in week one, as Ruksana did, even with an imperfect outline, would have given her something to submit.

qa.q: How might Ruksana have seen Dilnaz's weeks of preparation?
qa.a: Ruksana, writing from week one with fewer notes, may have admired the research but wondered why Dilnaz never began.

grounding: Shows a young adult researching and refining an outline for weeks without starting, preparation that felt productive but postponed being judged.
